articles.title: The Ambiguity Spiral in Iran
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ERIK LIN-GREENBERG is an Associate Professor in the Department of Political Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Ambiguity—vague language, mixed messaging, frequent policy shifts—has been a hallmark of the United States’ approach to the war in Iran. From almost the moment the conflict began, U.S. President Donald Trump has vacillated over its purpose, what risks he might be willing to take, and what the United States would consider victory. He has threatened to destroy Iranian civilization, then promptly signed a cease-fire agreement. He has floated the possibility of taking Kharg Island, the hub of Iran’s oil industry, only to quickly walk it back. And he has discussed imposing a 20 percent toll on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, only to declare that the waterway must be free to everyone.
In some cases, ambiguity can help countries settle wars. Leaders, for example, can leverage uncertainty to de-escalate a conflict or reach a stable peace agreement by letting both sides claim victory. If governments avoid drawing clear redlines, they can avoid pressure to escalate in response to attacks, creating space to cool tensions.
But Washington’s mixed messaging about the war in Iran has done more harm than good. Trump’s spectrum of threats, for example, prompted Tehran to see the war in existential terms and maximally fight back. The lack of clarity over the status of the Strait of Hormuz made the June memorandum of understanding negotiated by the two countries impossibly frail. To reach a more durable truce, the Trump administration needs to be clearer about its goals and more consistent in pursuing them. Otherwise, Iran and the United States will continue to get their wires crossed—and the next cease-fire could again collapse.
When coercing a rival, a government must decide how to convey intent, capabilities, and redlines. One option is to be clear: explicitly and consistently defining a goal, identifying consequences for noncompliance, and articulating what the other side can count on if demands are met. Such clarity can let a rival state know what is at stake and encourage it to limit its response. But too much of it can do the opposite. If the rival knows just how far it can go toward a threshold without triggering retaliation, it will often escalate all the way to that point.
The other option is to be vague. Yet this can also have mixed consequences. If a state does not know how its adversary will respond to a certain action, it might hold back for fear of triggering painful counterattacks. But too many mixed signals can throw off an opponent’s risk calculus, giving rise to misunderstandings that can produce or worsen a crisis.
This is what happened with the United States’ Operation Epic Fury—its military operation against Iran. Trump has variously said, at different times, that the goal of the campaign is to degrade Iran’s missile capabilities and navy, prevent the country from obtaining nuclear weapons, and end Iran’s support of its regional proxy network. On the first day of the conflict, he even suggested he wanted to dismantle the Islamic Republic. (On February 28, Trump encouraged Iranians to “take over” their government, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has carried out military strikes alongside Trump, echoed that sentiment.) Other Trump administration officials, meanwhile, avoided explicit mention of a political transformation for Iran, focusing on narrower military objectives.
For Iran, this mixed messaging was the opposite of reassuring. Uncertain of U.S. intentions, its officials assumed the worst—particularly given that airstrikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the conflict’s opening hours. The country thus escalated massively, unleashing thousands of missiles and drones at infrastructure and U.S. military bases across the Middle East. If the United States had been clear from the outset that it was not gunning for regime change, Iran might have responded with more restraint and the conflict might have stayed more limited, as it had after U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on Iran in June 2025.
Ambiguity has not only ramped up the conflict. It has also undermined efforts at ending it. The June memorandum of understanding was meant to pause fighting, open the Strait of Hormuz, and start a 60-day period for further negotiations. But it failed, in part because of its unclear wording. The memorandum obliged Iran to “make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels.” The Americans interpreted this clause to mean that Iran would let all traffic through, as it did before the war. The Iranians, on the other hand, took it as a confirmation that they had authority over the waterway and only needed to open parts of it. (Iran wants shipping to pass through the part of the strait closest to its territory). At the end of June, Iran began shooting at commercial vessels for taking what it deemed to be unauthorized routes through the channel. As these attacks unfolded, Iran’s deputy foreign minister took to social media to announce that safe passage was “not guaranteed under vague arrangements.” The United States interpreted these strikes as violations of the cease-fire, so it responded by firing at Iran. A similar tit for tat played out in mid-July, resulting in the fighting that continues today.
Although all conflicts are confusing and chaotic to some degree—hence the term “fog of war”—the one in Iran seems particularly ambiguous. Much of this ambiguity stems not from a calculated strategy to leverage obscurity for military or political gain, but from Washington’s struggle to settle on a desired end state. Deliberate ambiguity increases uncertainty by keeping opponents guessing. But when a country is ambiguous about its direction because of internal indecision, it tends to routinely back down from threats only to reissue them, eroding its credibility instead of merely throwing off opponents.
Still, the Trump administration is not fully to blame for the United States’ ambiguous posture. There are factors outside its control that undercut the White House’s ability to send clear and credible signals to Iran. Weak domestic support for the war, for example, makes it harder to convincingly threaten Tehran. According to July polling by The Washington Post and Ipsos, 68 percent of Americans believe that the war is “not worth fighting.” Tehran is well aware of this fact, which functions as a caveat to all of Trump’s statements. Even when the president makes seemingly clear and direct threats, Iranian officials cannot be sure he will follow through, given his domestic political constraints. Iran, in turn, may feel emboldened to brush off the administration’s threats and demands.
The United States’ relationship with its partners in the region also clouds its messaging and invites escalation. American armed forces launched the war alongside Israel, which has different interests, redlines, and objectives. In April, for example, Washington and Tehran signed a two-week cease-fire to stop the fighting, but Israel’s obligations under the pact were unclear. The Iranians said the deal required Israel to halt attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon; Israel argued that operations in Lebanon fell outside the pact’s remit. Washington backed its ally, and Israel ramped up strikes on Hezbollah targets. Tehran in turn accused American leaders of “oath-breaking” and likely concluded that the United States was not a credible negotiating partner because it could not stop its regional ally. Iran retaliated with missile attacks on Israel weeks later.
Although ambiguity has been an escalatory force in the war with Iran, that does not mean it always worsens conflict. At times, it provides policymakers with room to maneuver, to downplay hostility, or to exaggerate their own accomplishments. Indeed, U.S. officials have, on occasion, leveraged ambiguity to achieve this very effect. Weeks after the April cease-fire was signed, Tehran launched drones and missiles at American warships in the Strait of Hormuz. This could easily have triggered a descent back into full-scale conflict. Yet because the exact terms of the April cease-fire were never publicly released, Trump was able to downplay the incident. The president told reporters that Iran had merely “trifled with us,” insisting the truce remained intact. When the United States launched retaliatory strikes, Trump soft-pedaled their significance, referring to them as “just a love tap.” Central Command similarly announced that it did “not seek escalation.” Iran appeared to accept that narrative and held off on more strikes.
Moreover, whether intentional or the result of incoherent policy, ambiguity can allow both Washington and Tehran to claim wins. For instance, because the Trump administration has offered a variety of aims for its war, it was able to claim it had successfully achieved several core objectives upon signing the June memorandum—destroying Iran’s missile capacity, degrading its navy, and limiting the reach of Tehran’s proxies—even though the military campaign had failed to compel Iran to change regimes or abandon its nuclear pursuits. Iranian leaders, for their part, could declare that they succeeded by virtue of staying in power, inflicting damage on U.S. and Gulf infrastructure, and demonstrating their chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz.
These mutual declarations of victory ultimately could not save the memorandum. But similar assertions have de-escalated past crises. When Iran launched a barrage of missiles and drones at Israel in April 2024, Israel highlighted its success at defending its territory before retaliating with precision strikes against Iranian military targets. Iran’s government and media glossed over the damage caused by Israeli attacks and focused public attention on the fact that it had directly struck Israel for the first time. The lack of a clear outcome meant both sides could claim success, averting escalation.
A deliberate degree of ambiguity could also help end this conflict. If American and Iranian leaders keep their redlines vague when dealing with low-level military interactions, they will create off-ramps. But on the whole, the best way for the United States to settle the war with Iran is to be clearer about its objectives. The goals of Iran’s regime are evident: to maintain its grip on power at home, deter future attacks from its enemies, keep control over the Strait of Hormuz, secure release of frozen funds, and gain relief from sanctions. If Washington can sharpen its demands and communicate them consistently, both sides will be better able to focus negotiations and develop more viable plans for implementation—leading to a more durable agreement.
articles.summary: How Trump’s lack of clarity leads to escalation.

articles.title: Why a Weaker Russia Keeps Fighting
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ALEXANDER GABUEV is Director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin.
ALEXANDRA PROKOPENKO is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin. She worked at Russia’s central bank until early 2022.
TATIANA STANOVAYA is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center and the Founder and CEO of the political analysis firm R.Politik.
At the end of June, Russian President Vladimir Putin gave an interview in which he declared, once again, that Russia would win its war against Ukraine. The Russian army, he said, was advancing along the roughly 800-mile frontline and occupying more Ukrainian land every day. Kyiv, by contrast, was flailing. He acknowledged that the Ukrainian drone strikes torching Russian oil refineries and other critical infrastructure deep behind the frontlines were “creating problems.” But Russians would adapt and persevere. “These terrorist attacks have no impact whatsoever on the situation,” he said.
If this were 20 months ago, Putin’s confidence would have been warranted. At the time, recently elected U.S. President Donald Trump was praising Moscow and criticizing Kyiv. Russian troops were making slow but steady gains on the battlefield. Putin could thus follow three strategies, as we argued in a March 2025 Foreign Affairs essay. Under Plan A, the Kremlin would work with the White House to make Kyiv accept a deal written in Moscow. Under Plan B, Putin would simply hold out until Trump pulled U.S. support for Ukraine, allowing Russian troops to roll to victory. Failing that, Putin could pivot to Plan C: continuing to fight and ultimately prevailing on the battlefield.
Today, however, Russia’s position has deteriorated. Plan A—winning over Trump—failed; Putin didn’t even mention the U.S. president in his recent interview. Plan B also went awry. Although the White House stopped providing Ukraine with many types of assistance, the United States has continued to supply vital intelligence to Kyiv and enforce sanctions against Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv has been able to turn to its European backers to make up for the lost aid. In fact, Ukraine is now better positioned militarily than it was last year. Russia, by contrast, is losing more soldiers than it can recruit and stalling out on the battlefield. Its economy is facing increasing trouble. Thus, Plan C, in which Russia would win by outlasting Ukraine, is also not working.
But that does not mean Putin will change course. Russia’s problems are real, but the country is nonetheless capable of sustaining the conflict. Its economy remains functional enough, and it has the manpower and weaponry needed to keep battling. Moscow is also devising new ways to regain the initiative. The Kremlin’s insistence on continuing to fight will make life worse for Russians, and so there are elites in Moscow calling for a negotiated resolution. But there is no indication that Putin is listening. The war, then, is almost certain to drag on.
When Trump took office in 2025, the Kremlin believed it could achieve a diplomatic coup. During the 2024 campaign, Trump had pledged to end the war in Ukraine “within 24 hours.” Upon taking office, he moved to pressure Ukraine’s leaders to accede to some of Russia’s demands. In February 2025, he insisted that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky agree to an immediate cease-fire with Russia and insinuated that Kyiv was responsible for the war. When Zelensky refused, Trump temporarily suspended intelligence sharing and military aid to Ukraine. Vice President JD Vance delivered a speech at the 2025 Munich Security Conference in which he declared that the United States was pulling back from Europe. And in August 2025, Trump and Putin held an amiable summit in Alaska. Afterward, the U.S. president said, again, that Zelensky was the reason the conflict wasn’t finished.
The trajectory of the Russian economy and the dynamics of the battlefield further boosted Putin’s confidence. In 2024, Russia’s GDP grew by 4.3 percent, fueled by military production and domestic consumption. Inflation was high but manageable. The Russian armed forces were recruiting more men than they were losing, whereas the Ukrainian army was losing more soldiers than it was gaining. The creeping occupation of the Donbas was costing Russia tens of thousands of troops, but these losses were tolerated as the country continued to advance. In 2024, Putin captured around 1,600 square miles of Ukrainian territory. Russia was producing nearly as many drones as Ukraine and using them in increasingly creative ways. It was producing far more traditional weapons, such as artillery shells and missiles, than was Ukraine or its Western partners. From the Kremlin’s viewpoint, a Russian victory was inevitable.
But not for the first time, Putin’s complacency led to overconfidence. He continued to push for conditions that Trump either could not accept or could not deliver—including that Kyiv surrender parts of the Donbas it still controlled and sign away much of its sovereignty. Trump’s two main envoys to Moscow, his friend Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, were amateurs in international diplomacy and proved unable to start a proper negotiating process. In Moscow, attitudes toward both men soured. Plan A failed.
For a time, Putin could still hope that Plan B, in which Trump would simply wash his hands of Ukraine, would succeed. In March 2025, Trump permanently stopped supplying Ukraine with free U.S. weapons, dealing a blow to Kyiv. By July 2025, he had zeroed out American financial assistance to the country. But smart diplomacy by Ukrainian officials and their European allies ultimately persuaded Trump to keep sharing intelligence with Kyiv and to continue selling weapons to Ukraine via a program paid for by Europe. The Europeans also stepped in to provide Ukraine with the financial assistance Washington had yanked, and they turned the continent into the secure rear of Ukraine’s defense industrial base—providing money, technology, and safe locations in EU territory for Ukraine to manufacture its own drones and missiles. At the same time, Trump grew frustrated with Putin over Russia’s failure to entertain any concessions. He kept existing sanctions against Russia in place and even blacklisted the Kremlin’s two largest oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, putting pressure on Putin’s war chest.
With the failure of Plans A and B, Putin proceeded to Plan C—winning the war on the battlefield. Yet this plan is beginning to falter, as well. The war effort itself is clearly floundering: in 2025, the Russian army captured more than 1,600 square miles of Ukrainian territory (at a tremendously high cost in terms of casualties), but in the first half of this year, it advanced, at most, around 250 square miles. That is, in part, because Ukraine has built additional lines of defense with fortifications and minefields. It is also because Ukrainians have been able to expand what analysts call the “kill zone,” or the area along the frontlines where Russian soldiers are almost immediately detected by Ukraine’s drones and then hit.
The result has been even greater Russian fatalities. Although public data is unavailable, according to the Carnegie Endowment military analyst Michael Kofman, the number of Russian soldiers killed each month has almost certainly risen dramatically over the last 18 months. Taken together, the number of Russian troops either killed or grievously wounded each month sits at roughly 30,000. Meanwhile, the number of troops who join each month has fallen to 27,000—the result of dwindling sign-up bonuses in some Russian regions and a growing awareness of the death count. Moscow’s ability to decisively breach the Ukrainian frontline is increasingly in doubt.
The Kremlin is facing other troubles, too. Ukraine has carried out a highly successful midrange strike campaign that has disrupted Russian logistics and supply lines, further slowing the Russian military’s advance. Kyiv has scaled up its long-range strike campaign, hitting military production facilities and civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia, including oil ports and refineries. Thanks to these attacks, about one-third of Russian oil-refining capacity is offline, causing gasoline shortages, fuel rationing, and long lines at the pumps that lasted from June until late July, and that will likely return when Ukraine restarts these strikes. In July, Ukraine started blowing up warehouses belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, making the war top of mind for ordinary consumers and affecting the thousands of Russian small and medium businesses that sell via the retail firm. Kyiv has also intensified efforts to isolate Crimea by targeting fuel supply routes and power generation facilities in the occupied peninsula. And Ukrainian drones are attacking Russian oil tankers and cargo vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an attempt to stop the country’s maritime oil and grain exports.
Kyiv’s campaign is damaging Russia’s economy. The official 2026 forecast for Russian GDP growth is a meager 0.4 percent. Inflation is on the rise. To avoid even higher prices, the country’s central bank is keeping the interest rate at 14 percent. But this punishing figure makes credit prohibitively expensive for many businesses. Most worrying of all for the Kremlin, the budget deficit has swelled by $73 billion in the first six months of 2026, far exceeding the $48.5 billion it had anticipated for the entire year. Trump’s war against Iran has increased Russian oil revenues, but these inflows are not nearly enough to produce a cash cushion, and the monetary reserves Russia accumulated from decades of commodities exports, including from the war-induced commodities price boom in 2022, are gone. In order to finance its growing war bill, the Kremlin has to keep cutting nonmilitary expenditures and borrow domestically, right as Russian bond buyers are requesting higher risk premiums.
Thanks to these troubles, the Kremlin is losing support at home. The economic difficulties, energy blackouts, Internet restrictions, and general wartime fatigue have pushed Putin’s approval ratings from around 80 percent at the beginning of the year to 66 percent in mid-July. All available polling data indicates that the public mood in Russia is growing more uncertain and anxious. The country is becoming less and less convinced that its soldiers can win and that Putin has a realistic plan.
Given all these failures, Western governments might think that Putin would be willing to consider a meaningful settlement. But sadly, there is little to suggest this is the case. In fact, in all his recent public appearances, Putin has indicated that his war aims haven’t changed at all. “Unable to defeat Russia on the battlefield, our adversaries are resorting to outright terrorist methods against our people,” he declared on July 27. “But the people of Russia can never be broken.”
Unfortunately, Putin still has the power to back up such statements. The Russian economy may be struggling, but it is not on the verge of collapse. Moscow can keep paying for the war by forcing businesses to absorb the cost of drone attacks rather than spending on better drone defenses or compensating damaged firms. It can make regional governments absorb rising defense costs via smaller budgets, and it can compel households to absorb war costs in the form of higher inflation. The Kremlin can cut more civilian expenditures from the national budget, too. Right now, Russia is spending eight percent of its GDP on defense—a high figure—but far less than what the Soviet Union or the United States spent during World War II, or the nearly 40 percent Ukraine is spending right now.
These policies will make Russians angrier and poorer. But the Kremlin is insulated from mounting dissatisfaction. The regime has sophisticated tools of repression, including blanket censorship laws, AI-powered surveillance tools, and expanded law enforcement agencies, that can contain any outbursts. Public frustration with the economy might also be offset by a growing rally-around-the-flag effect. As Ukrainian attacks intensify and affect more people, ordinary Russians may well conclude that the war against Kyiv is a war for national survival, just as Putin has long suggested. Polling by the independent Levada Center shows that support for the actions of the Russian armed forces sits above 65 percent nationwide, with less than 25 percent of the population opposed. But in Russian regions bordering Ukraine, which started to face Kyiv’s retaliatory strikes earlier than the rest of the country, support for the war is even higher.
Moscow, of course, could have wide domestic backing and a stable economy and still be forced to settle if its military starts to fall apart. But the Kremlin has ways to maintain its strengths on the battlefield. Moscow continues to increase its production of glide bombs, which threaten Ukrainian military positions and terrorize cities close to the frontline—including regional capitals such as Zaporizhzhia or Sumy. Russia has also doubled its production of ballistic missiles from prewar levels, just as Ukraine has run low on high-quality interceptors (a shortage exacerbated by Washington’s decision to go to war against Iran and, thus, no longer sell Patriots to Ukraine), which gives Putin an opportunity to bombard Ukrainian cities with missiles carrying much bigger payloads than drones. This will be particularly devastating during the winter, when Ukraine will most be in need of electricity, and when Russia can cause the most harm. The Kremlin has also started to systematically target Ukrainian ports and ships in the Black Sea in hopes of degrading the infrastructure that supports the country’s agricultural exports. Putin believes that if he inflicts enough terror on Ukrainian civilians, he can compel a new, massive wave of migrants to flee the country for Europe ahead of regional elections in Germany and a presidential election in France, bolstering anti-Ukraine, far-right parties in both places and pushing the continent away from Kyiv.
Should this bombing campaign alone not be enough to turn the tide and force Kyiv to accept Putin’s demands, the Kremlin can increase the pressure by mobilizing more men. Putin has mobilized the country once, in late 2022, when he conscripted people from across the country’s provinces. This succeeded at generating hundreds of thousands of new troops, but it led to a temporary drop in Putin’s approval rating and an exodus of hundreds of thousands of military-age men. In response, he switched to using cash incentives. But now that this system is reaching its limits, the regime is preparing to switch back to conscription—this time relying on electronic draft notices that are quieter and can be sent out year-round to thousands of potential conscripts. These conscripts, unlike the ones of 2022, would be blocked at the border if they tried to leave Russia. The country’s law enforcement agencies could also use digital surveillance cameras and facial recognition tools to search for draft dodgers and threaten them with a (newly introduced) two-year prison sentence. The mobilization will almost certainly cause some renewed discontent, but the process will be far less flashy than in 2022, when Putin went on national TV and announced a mobilization, and will thus attract less attention. The Kremlin is also likely to make sure that the mobilization effort largely skips over the capital and other large cities, and instead focuses on poorer areas.
Moscow can also further increase the pressure on Europe. It could carry out more hybrid attacks, or deniable military operations that fall short of outright warfare but still damage or threaten a target. Throughout the previous four years, Russia has, for example, sent drones and clandestine operatives to disrupt European defense production facilities, military bases, and transport infrastructure. (It denies responsibility for all these attacks.) But it could expand its list of targets in hopes of further disrupting life for ordinary Europeans, including by damaging commercial warehouses with cheap drones.
Not everyone in the Russian establishment wants to continue the war, let alone escalate it. Among the country’s elite, one can now find voices calling for genuine negotiations. ln May, for example, Russia’s flagship foreign affairs journal published an article by Vasily Kashin, a prominent, pragmatic but nationalistic military analyst, that made the case for freezing the conflict. Russia, Kashin argued, could not achieve more on the battlefield in the short to medium term, and the costs of prolonged war were starting to outstrip strategic benefits. Given the journal’s prominence, Kashin’s article was almost certainly previewed and green-lighted by officials in the Kremlin, likely as a way of giving voice to the pragmatists in the Russian security establishment. Likewise, on June 30, the CEO of Russia’s largest bank (and a longtime Putin lieutenant) suggested that it was time to wrap up the conflict. “I don’t think there is a single person in the country who has any concerns other than the swiftest conclusion of the hostilities,” he said.
But this option is currently of no interest to Putin. Although he tolerates cautious calls for peace and sometimes sends signals that he is interested in a settlement, too, Putin’s actions suggest that he is not ready to crawl out of the hole he is now in. In fact, he seems to want to keep digging. As long as Putin is convinced that he has an advantage over Ukraine with the destructiveness of his ballistic missiles and that Ukraine is vulnerable because of its lack of interceptors, he is likely to keep trying to wear Ukraine down—no matter the damage to his country. He views uncoordinated calls from Americans and Europeans for talks or for a cease-fire as a ploy to buy Ukraine more time. “We know that the West continues to pursue Russia’s strategic defeat,” he said in the June 28 interview. “Why are they calling for a cease-fire and peace negotiations? . . . If Ukraine is, as they claim, capturing more and more territory . . . then Western leaders simply need to wait. Russia’s strategic defeat would, it would seem, come about of its own accord.”
Ukraine and its allies need to prepare for a long and bumpy road. Kyiv may be in the best position in the war since late 2022, but the Kremlin believes it will crush the will of Ukraine and its friends this winter. Russia may be struggling, but Putin has not exhausted his options. He still wants to fight for as long as possible.
articles.summary: Putin sees little need to negotiate.

articles.title: The Next Phase of China’s Minority Crackdown
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
JAMES LEIBOLD is Emeritus Professor at La Trobe University.
TENZIN DORJEE is Director of Research and Advocacy at Tibet Action Institute.
When the People’s Republic of China was founded, in 1949, it was explicitly a multinational state. Although Han Chinese make up more than 90 percent of the country’s population, China’s constitution and subsequent laws grant minority nationalities autonomy in specific regions and promise them collective agency as “masters of their own homes.” For decades, the party-state’s official bargain—honored unevenly and often violated—was that national unity would be best secured by recognizing difference and granting minorities limited territorial, linguistic, and political autonomy within China, rather than by forcing them to be absorbed into Han culture.
As of July 1, however, national integration through forced cultural assimilation is the law of the land. The constitution still defines the country as a multinational state, but the passage of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress marks a decisive turn away from the promise of territorial autonomy. It codifies the coercive project to create a Chinese national community in which minority peoples can exist only insofar as they serve Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s vision of China—a vision rooted in the belief that commonality is better than diversity and that national cohesion requires a single shared Chinese cultural and linguistic identity.
The new ethnic unity law did not introduce the policy of assimilation; for more than a decade, Xi has been replacing minority-language education with Mandarin Chinese instruction, increasing the party’s control over religion, and recasting minority histories as strands of one continuous Chinese civilization. But this approach is now consolidated in national legislation enacted by the full National People’s Congress, signaling that Beijing regards it as a matter of fundamental state importance and enshrining it with the highest legal authority. And the law distributes responsibility for implementing these policies across all levels of the state and throughout society.
Beijing’s campaign of cultural dispossession will now become more deeply embedded in bureaucratic practices and institutional structures, which are difficult to dislodge or change. Even if a more liberal leader were to one day succeed Xi, reviving autonomy would require a complete bureaucratic, political, and cultural overhaul. For the foreseeable future, therefore, Beijing has closed the door on peaceful coexistence, locking itself instead into a more hostile and zero-sum relationship with the minority groups whose cultures and languages it once accommodated.
China’s official policy, inspired by the Soviet model of national-territorial autonomy, recognizes 56 formally equal nationalities within the country. Its constitution promises to protect the rights and interests of all minority nationalities and grants them territorial autonomy in areas where they live in concentrated communities. A 1984 law formalized the protections and accommodations granted to minority groups as part of this territorial autonomy. In areas as varied as Xinjiang in the far northwest and Yunnan in the country’s southwest, minority groups were entitled to use their own languages as the medium of instruction in schools and maintain their own traditions, cultures, and religious practices. Even when these protections were violated, the law maintained the principle of collective rights for China’s non-Han nationalities.
But Xi began systematically dismantling the foundations of this system soon after he became general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party in 2012. His move to dismantle territorial autonomy is often explained as a response to episodes of unrest that broke out in minority regions shortly before he took power. In 2008, protests that began in Lhasa, the capital of Tibet, escalated into a full-blown uprising across the plateau. And in 2009, a Uyghur protest in Urumqi, in Xinjiang, descended into rioting and retaliatory violence that killed nearly 200 people, according to official figures.
The roots of Xi’s campaign, however, go back much further. The collapse of the Soviet Union in the 1990s prompted some leading Chinese scholars and officials to reconsider granting territorial autonomy to minority nationalities. Starting around the first decade of the twenty-first century, advocates of a so-called second-generation ethnic policy argued that China’s Soviet-inspired approach had hardened ethnic boundaries and created the conditions for separatism. They warned that minority groups’ distinct identities, institutions, and languages were impeding China’s attempt to construct a cohesive nation. Although the situation in Beijing is fundamentally different than it was in Moscow—China’s autonomous regions are much more tightly controlled by the central government and possess neither sovereignty nor a legal route to independence, as federal republics in the Soviet Union did—these powerful voices warned that even limited autonomy was dangerous. China’s existing policy, they argued, was putting it at risk of sharing the fate of the Soviet Union, which had disintegrated along the borders of its nationality-based republics.
Xi’s nation-building project has grown out of their radical thesis. Xi has insisted on dismantling and weakening the minority languages, religious institutions, and historical memories that might sustain any claims to collective self-rule. He has sought to remake the inner life of China’s non-Han peoples so that claims to distinct political identity become harder to imagine, mobilize, or transmit. The Mongolian scholar Uradyn Bulag has called this “politicide”—the destruction of a people’s capacity to understand itself and act as a distinct political community.
This campaign of assimilation has ensnared all minority groups, but it has especially targeted the three nationalities most culturally distinct from the Han majority: Mongols, Tibetans, and Uyghurs. Starting in 2017, authorities in Xinjiang detained an estimated one million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in political reeducation camps. Beijing has placed nearly a million Tibetan children in state-run boarding schools, including preschools, where separation from their families and education predominantly conducted in Mandarin weaken the intergenerational transmission of culture. And in 2020, when Inner Mongolia required key school subjects to be taught in Mandarin, Mongolian students and parents organized boycotts and demonstrations; party authorities responded by detaining protesters, pressuring families to send their children back to school, punishing teachers, and purging Mongolian officials from party leadership positions.
The effects of these efforts are visible. The nationalist newspaper Global Times reported as early as 2016 that some Tibetan children were losing the ability to converse easily with parents and grandparents, and videos shared over social media in recent months show children struggling to pronounce their own names in Tibetan. For Beijing, such episodes suggest that forced assimilation is working as intended. In the logic of Xi and his intellectual forebears, the erasure of distinct cultural and linguistic identities will make it harder for a territorially based separatist movement to gain traction.
But until July 1, these assimilationist policies had a problem: they violated legal promises that the state had made to its citizens. Xi has now narrowed this inconvenient gap between law and policy. He did not repeal the existing framework guaranteeing autonomy, which formally remains in place. Instead, he imposed a new statutory framework that institutionalizes cultural assimilation, emptying autonomy of any substantive meaning.
The new ethnic unity law makes Mandarin Chinese the basic language of education and official life across China. It says that museums, heritage sites, public buildings, and place names are required to display “shared Chinese cultural symbols,” and requires state officials to use new technologies, including artificial intelligence, to promote a standardized image of the Chinese nation. Even family life is drawn into the project: parents and guardians of minority children are told to educate them to love the party, the motherland, and the Chinese nation. Those who violate the law, including individuals and organizations outside China, are said to be creating “ethnic division” and may face administrative penalties, detention, or even criminal prosecution.
The law presents itself as a measure to strengthen national cohesion. At its heart is one of Xi’s signature formulations: “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” In English, the phrase sounds benign—a type of civic nationalism with Chinese characteristics. But in Chinese, the wording carries a far more assertive and directional connotation: “forging” is the same word used to describe casting molten ore into unbreakable iron. In Xi’s usage, the goal is not only to encourage loyalty to the party-state but also to mold individual consciousness itself. It is, in the official language of the party, the forging and casting of souls—that is, the remaking of habits, attachments, and historical memories that national minorities in China rely on to understand who they are and where they belong.
The stakes of the law can be understood through the political theorist Will Kymlicka’s distinction between colonized national minorities and immigrant communities. In many liberal societies, immigrants seek equal citizenship, protection from discrimination, and accommodation of distinct cultural or religious practices. National minorities, by contrast, were involuntarily incorporated into new states. They ground their claims to collective continuity and self-government in ancestral territory, language, and inherited institutions. Their demand is not only to be included as individuals but also to preserve and transmit their collective identity across generations.
Many Mongols, Tibetans, and Uyghurs are not willing to trade partial assimilation for equal opportunity. These groups’ repeated street demonstrations—even in the face of harsh state retaliation—have made it clear that what they want, at a minimum, is some level of genuine autonomy in China or a way to preserve their unique cultures. What the new law enforces, under the guise of civic inclusion, is a requirement that they become part of a single, party-defined Chinese identity. It sends the message that the languages, histories, and identities of China’s non-Han citizens will not be tolerated unless they can be folded into a single Chinese national story.
The law does not prohibit diversity, and officials are likely to welcome ethnic costumes, food, and music—at least where they can be packaged and commercialized as colorful performances for Han tourists and party officials, or displayed as evidence of China’s supposedly harmonious pluralism. But this is diversity reduced to spectacle. It will be carefully curated and mostly detached from the communities that produce it. If it challenges Han Chinese norms, suggests a distinct collective identity, or supports claims to meaningful self-rule, it will not be tolerated.
Minority communities that seek to maintain their culture will be pushed toward a double life of public conformity and private preservation. Language instruction, religious practice, and historical memory are likely to retreat further into homes, rely more on informal networks, and increasingly center on diaspora institutions based outside mainland China, widening the gap between official performances of unity and experiences of coercion.
Xi may believe that the new law will secure political stability for generations by reducing the possibility of separatism. But turning the project of cultural homogenization into law may end up backfiring. For decades, prominent figures such as the Dalai Lama, the Han writer Wang Lixiong, and the Uyghur economist Ilham Tohti occupied a shrinking political middle ground between assimilation and independence. They argued, in different ways, that meaningful autonomy, not independence, offered a realistic path to interethnic reconciliation. With enough autonomy, they believed, minority groups could coexist peacefully with the Chinese state without sacrificing their culture or challenging Beijing’s authority.
By formally hollowing out the autonomy it once promised, Beijing is closing off the possibility of such a settlement. The party claims exclusive authority to select and recognize the successor to the Dalai Lama; Wang’s work is barred from publication in China, and he has been prevented from leaving the country since 2015; and Tohti is serving a life sentence in a Chinese prison on trumped-up charges of separatism.
Rather than ensure stability, a program of coercive integration can harden political claims that survive beyond the state’s reach. In the late Soviet Union, for example, backlash against Russification helped fuel national mobilization, especially in the Baltic republics, where reform movements eventually became independence movements. And in Yugoslavia, the former Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic’s move to dismantle Kosovo’s autonomy, in 1989, became a symbol of Serbian centralization and helped destroy confidence in the federal compact that promised cultural and linguistic accommodation.
China’s far greater coercive capacity makes comparable mobilization inside the country unlikely, at least for now. But as Beijing eliminates the possibility of meaningful autonomy for minority nationalities inside China, demands for independence are likely to grow among Mongolian, Tibetan, and Uyghur activists in exile. On July 2, one day after China’s new law took effect, Tibetan independence activist Lobga Rangzen set himself on fire outside the United Nations headquarters in New York to protest Chinese rule over Tibet. A single tragic act does not make a trend, but the self-immolation captures the polarizing effect of destroying the middle ground between assimilation and separation. By dismantling autonomy, Xi may find that his only option for preserving national unity is a state of permanent coercion.
articles.summary: Forced assimilation is now the law.

articles.title: The New Old Middle East
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
In many ways, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and the war in Gaza that preceded it seem transformative. After decades of shadow warfare, Iran and Israel have now attacked each other’s homelands directly. And Israel and the United States have joined forces in a genuinely novel way to wage war against Iran. The Islamic Republic has lost its supreme leader of 36 years and much of its defense infrastructure. The Gulf states, once largely able to stay out of harm’s way, have seen their energy facilities, airports, and hotels go up in flames. Hezbollah has dragged Lebanon, which was just starting to recover from its last war, back into conflict. The Assad regime, which had ruled Syria for nearly half a century, was swept away when its partners in Beirut and Tehran were battered and unable to offer any help. Israel, for its part, has flattened Gaza, tiptoed toward annexing the West Bank, reoccupied parts of southern Lebanon, and extended its control of Syrian territory beyond the Golan Heights.
All these changes are real and important, and they have caused millions of people to suffer. Yet overall, the Middle East emerging out of this upheaval looks a lot like the one that existed before it. Outsiders continue to play their balance-of-power games within the borders of weak Arab states, the Iranian-Israeli conflict endures, the Palestinian question remains unresolved, and the United States lacks the capacity or the will to impose order but is still too involved in the region to leave.
The cease-fire signed by Iran and the United States in June 2026 captures the Trump administration’s failure to fundamentally alter the region. After suffering a series of blows between 2023 and 2025, Tehran has affirmed its power by exercising a chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz and assaulting its Gulf neighbors. The prewar regime in Tehran is largely intact and is now dominated by members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who are just as committed as their predecessors to opposing Israel and meddling in weak Arab states. The U.S.-Israeli war that began in February 2026 was meant to sap Iran’s power, if not to eliminate its regime. Instead, it has given the Islamic Republic a new lease on life.
Despite two and a half years of fighting and the deaths of tens of thousands of people, mostly Palestinians, the situation in Israel, Gaza, and the West Bank is largely the same as it was before the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. Hamas has been defanged, but Israel’s extraordinary use of force has not solved the fundamental problems at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Although some Israeli officials favor the total expulsion of the Palestinians and the annexation of their territories, that has not occurred and will not occur any time soon. In the absence of a political settlement that involves some kind of Palestinian self-determination, the basic shape of the conflict remains the same. Israel shows no signs of contemplating the kind of compromises that might lead to such a settlement, and the United States has been reluctant to lean on Israel to make concessions.
The United States and Israel cannot bomb their way to a better region. A truly changed Middle East, one that could be the basis for a more stable regional order, would be defined by stronger central governments in Arab states such as Iraq, Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen. Today, those places are plagued by civil war or domestic unrest, and the region will remain volatile as long as those governments are not able to police their borders and prevent nonstate actors in their territories from pursuing their own foreign and military policies. Weak states, after all, cannot make durable peace.
A transformed Middle East would also see an end to the efforts of regional and outside powers, most notably but not exclusively Iran, to encourage or fund militias. It would include a diplomatic process, broadly supported internationally and accepted regionally, focused on working toward a settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict that would ensure Israel’s security and the Palestinians’ right to self-determination. And it might involve genuine regime change in Iran, carried out by the Iranians themselves and resulting in a government that respects its neighbors’ sovereignty and drops the ideological crusade against Israel.
The regional war that began in 2023 did not move the Middle East closer to that kind of transformation. At the time of this writing, Iran and the United States were alternating between negotiating and fighting each other, but neither was willing to escalate in a way that would change the fundamentals of the situation they’ve been in since February. Tehran will not allow free and unfettered shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, give up its nuclear program, or abandon its regional proxies. Washington seems unlikely to send troops to Iran, a prerequisite for externally imposed regime change. Unless the government in Tehran collapses by other means and is replaced by something radically different—an outcome that seems even less probable now than it did before the war started—then no matter how long the war goes on or how it eventually ends, the drama and bloodshed of the past years will amount to little more than sound and fury. And because there has been no meaningful change to the essential dynamics and interests of the Middle East, even if a more sustainable cease-fire is achieved, the countdown to the next war will have already begun.
Between October 7, 2023, and February 28, 2026, Iran suffered so many blows that it began to look like a paper tiger. Its nuclear infrastructure was reduced to rubble by Israeli and U.S. strikes in June 2025. Israel disrupted Iran from within, killing generals and nuclear scientists on Iranian soil and assassinating the Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran itself. Bashar al-Assad’s fall in Syria in December 2024 severed Iran’s land bridge to Lebanon. Israel devastated Iran’s most powerful proxies, Hamas and Hezbollah. Persistent economic problems triggered a wave of protests against the Iranian regime in December 2025 that the regime brutally suppressed. According to the Human Rights Activists News Agency, the regime’s security forces killed at least 7,000 protesters; other organizations put that number in the tens of thousands. Iran’s apparent weakness undoubtedly tempted U.S. President Donald Trump into thinking that more strikes could lead to regime change. When he launched attacks in conjunction with Israel on February 28 of this year, he urged Iranians to “take over” their government.
Yet Iran emerged victorious from this latest round of fighting. Of course, the country is still plagued by the same economic problems and social discontent that drove Iranians into the streets in December. But by defying a U.S.-Israeli onslaught and discovering its leverage over world energy markets, the Iranian regime has regained prominence. It will certainly continue with the fundamental elements of its regional policy of the past 47 years: opposition to Israel, resistance to American power, and involvement in the politics of weak Arab states. And it will have every incentive to do whatever it can to develop nuclear weapons as the ultimate deterrent to future attacks from Israel and the United States.
Iran’s allies, although weakened, still wield significant influence across the Arab world. In Iraq’s elections in November 2025, Shiite parties aligned with Iran and the Iraqi militias it backs performed well. In February, March, and April of this year, those militias lobbed missiles at U.S. bases in the region. The new Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, like its predecessors, has filled impor-tant positions with many of Iran’s local allies.
Israeli assaults on Hezbollah between 2023 and 2025 opened a brief window for the historically weak Lebanese government to assert itself. Joseph Aoun, a Maronite Christian and former general whose election had been blocked for years by Hezbollah, was chosen as president by Lebanon’s parliament in January 2025. Lebanon subsequently made some progress on implementing the 2024 cease-fire agreement with Israel: Hezbollah, for example, had mostly withdrawn from the Lebanese border with Israel by the end of 2025.
But the task of restoring the state’s primacy in Lebanon remained unfinished business as Hezbollah joined in Iran’s retaliatory strikes in response to the 2026 U.S.-Israeli campaign. Israel, in turn, launched a ground invasion of southern Lebanon and an air campaign across the entire country, killing over 4,200 people and displacing one million others. Although Hezbollah is Israel’s stated target, the victim of the campaign is more likely to be the new Lebanese government, which condemned Hezbollah’s attack and offered to negotiate with Israel. Hezbollah has survived more than 40 years of conflict with Israel, including this latest assault. The Lebanese government, however, is likely to be discredited because it was unable to prevent yet another enormous disruption to the lives of ordinary people.
The Houthis, Iran’s ally in Yemen, snarled global shipping, ostensibly in solidarity with the Palestinians, in the Bab el Mandeb Strait between 2023 and 2025 but stayed above the fray in the first half of 2026, despite the attacks on Iran. The lull came from the group’s budding relationship with Saudi Arabia. Between 2022 and July 2026, the Houthis maintained a cease-fire with their neighbor, and during that time Riyadh paid the salaries of Yemeni civil servants, many of whom work under Houthi control. The Houthis remain ideologically and politically committed to Tehran and now seem to be reengaging in the fight in support of their ally. At the time of this writing, the Houthis had declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, the effect of which on energy flows in the Red Sea is uncertain but unlikely to be good. Some kind of Yemeni political settlement would advance security in the Middle East, but the more likely outcome of recent events is for the Houthis to rejoin the regional conflict.
From 2023 to 2025, the Gulf Arab countries were largely bystanders in the regional war. Qatar had hosted Hamas leaders and provided funding to the organization, with Israeli and U.S. approval, for a number of years. But no other Gulf state was particularly upset to see Hamas and Hezbollah weakened. The ferocity of the Israeli campaign in Gaza did, however, raise the salience of the Palestinian issue among Arab populations, making any overt support for Israel a risky proposition. As Iran became more vulnerable, Gulf leaders grew more worried that Israel would try to assert regional military dominance. Those fears were exacerbated in September 2025, when Israel struck a residence in Qatar in an unsuccessful attempt to kill Hamas officials who were there to negotiate a U.S.-backed proposal.
For years, the Gulf countries have favored stability in their neighborhood so they can focus on attracting the tourism, trade, and foreign investment needed to reduce their extreme reliance on energy exports. War is bad for business, which is why Gulf governments kept a low profile during the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in June 2025 and lobbied the United States against attacking Iran in early 2026.
This restraint didn’t help the Gulf countries with Iran. When Israel and the United States began their war against Iran in February 2026, it was the Gulf that bore the brunt of Tehran’s retaliation. As these countries were battered, their mindsets began to shift. At the beginning of the conflict, Gulf leaders seemed annoyed with the United States for putting them in the cross hairs of Iranian retaliation. But eventually, many Gulf elites came around to the opinion that the United States should continue the war until Iran loses the ability to threaten its neighbors. They were disappointed on both ends of the conflict.
Mixed feelings are a common feature of alliances between a weak country and a strong one. Weaker partners often fear both entrapment in wars that the stronger partner initiates and abandonment by the strong partner in the face of their common enemy. The Gulf states offer textbook examples of this dynamic. The memorandum of understanding signed by Iran and the United States in June 2026, for example, raised fears of desertion because it neglected to mention the Gulf states or address Iranian missile and drone capabilities. All the Gulf states, however, supported the memorandum because they worried that further U.S. escalation would lead to renewed Iranian attacks on their territories. Their fears were realized when the cease-fire broke down.
Yet despite their frustration, the Gulf countries are unlikely to distance themselves from the United States any time soon. American technology and training underpin Gulf air defenses, which proved quite successful in fending off Iranian drones and missiles. Moreover, the Gulf states have no other security guarantor to which they can turn. China has shown no desire to play that kind of role and does not have the power projection capabilities it would need to do so. Russia has taken Iran’s side and is busy with its own war in Ukraine. And European countries and regional powers such as Egypt, Pakistan, and Turkey cannot match the United States in terms of fighting capability.
What has changed over the past three years is the Gulf’s view of Israel. For years, Gulf countries had been slowly starting to embrace Israel as a potential ally against Iran. Even Saudi Arabia was considering warmer ties. But that trend has now reversed, and momentum for expanding the Abraham Accords—a series of agreements in 2020 that normalized relations between Israel and a number of Arab countries—has stalled. The Gaza war has made it more politically risky for Arab leaders to openly work with Israel. Israel’s strike against Qatar and its pursuit of war against Iran have led Gulf leaders to doubt that Israel cares about their security at all. The only Gulf state that has recommitted to its relationship with Israel is the United Arab Emirates, which already had the strongest ties with Israel.
By the end of 2025, Israel rightly considered itself the victor of the regional wars. But the country has been unable to achieve its ambitious goal of bringing down the Iranian regime. The June 2026 U.S.-Iranian cease-fire left the Islamic Republic in power with enough military assets to assert itself across the broader region and without a concrete obligation to give up its nuclear program. Moreover, Washington agreed to Tehran’s demand that the cease-fire also apply in Lebanon, where Israel was continuing its assault on Hezbollah. Even when Israel did come out on top in the wars of the past three years, it showed no interest in converting its victories into diplomatic initiatives. Israel has decided to play regional disruptor, confident that its military prowess is enough to protect it indefinitely. That is a questionable bet, given that its hard power was similarly impressive before October 7.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has been crystal clear that it will not accept a role for the Palestinian Authority in Gaza, making a solution to post-Hamas governance there nearly impossible to achieve. Violence continues in Gaza itself. Israeli forces have killed over 1,000 Palestinians since the cease-fire went into effect in October 2025. The international force that Trump’s 20-point peace plan proposed to provide security in Gaza has yet to materialize. The plan calls for a committee of Palestinian technocrats to administer Gaza; as of July 2026, Israel had not allowed them to enter the territory. Hamas refuses to disarm, despite its commitment to do so in the October 2025 truce, and Israeli forces still occupy about 70 percent of the enclave. The Gaza cease-fire looks more like a respite in the conflict than an end to it. There is certainly no hint of a long-term political solution that could change the current dynamic.
Other countries are hesitant to get involved in Gaza, either as security forces or development partners, without a reputable Palestinian partner with whom they can work. The Palestinian Authority, for all its faults, is the only plausible option. But far from encouraging the PA to play a role in Gaza, Israel is undercutting its administrative functions in the West Bank. During 2025, Israeli soldiers and settlers killed 240 Palestinians in the West Bank, and Israel approved 54 new settlements there—the highest yearly number since the signing of the 1993 Oslo peace accords, a series of agreements meant to lead to a two-state solution. In February 2026, the government adopted new legislation making it easier for Israeli settlers to buy land in the West Bank, a step that Palestinians say violates the Oslo accords and accelerates what they see as the momentum toward annexation. The current Israeli government prioritizes territorial expansion and the weakening of Palestinian institutions over any possibility of stable governance in the West Bank and Gaza.
Netanyahu believes that Israel is safer when its neighbors are weak and divided. But he misses the fact that Israel’s peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, two consolidated states that can control their borders and prevent the rise of violent nonstate actors in their territory, have been the enduring pillars of Israel’s security for decades. Rather than embrace the prospect of a cooperative Lebanese government willing to work against Hezbollah, Israel renewed its war in Lebanon in 2026. In Syria, Israel captured a so-called buffer zone, encouraged Syrian Druze to resist the new government, armed Druze militias, and struck Syrian army positions—including the headquarters of the Ministry of Defense—in the name of protecting the Druze.
Netanyahu obstructs state-building efforts in Lebanon and Syria in spite of U.S. efforts to support the new governments in Beirut and Damascus. Although Washington has admonished Israel on this score, Israeli policy has not substantially changed. Only when Israel’s hubris led it to bomb Qatar in September 2025 did Trump bring Netan-yahu to heel, forcing him to apologize publicly to the emir of Qatar and finally pressuring him to accept a cease-fire in Gaza. Washington needs to similarly pressure Israel to allow the new governments in Beirut and Damascus to reassert their control within their borders and build stronger state institutions.
By far the most significant geopolitical change brought about by the past three years of war was the fall of the Assad regime in Syria and the establishment of a new government led by Ahmed al-Shara, who was once a member of al-Qaeda. Since taking Syria’s capital, Shara has cultivated support from the United States, Turkey, the EU, and the Arab world, distancing Syria from the Iranian alliance that the Assad regime had maintained since the 1980s. These changes have also considerably reduced Iran’s ability to affect Lebanese politics and threaten Israel from Syrian territory, a real blow to Tehran’s regional influence.
Shara has said all the right things since coming to power, pledging a tolerant, consultative, and eventually democratic regime. His reassuring words aside, Syria remains deeply divided and traumatized after 14 years of brutal civil war. The forces allied with the new government have clashed with the Alawite minority in the west, the Druze in the south, and the Kurds in the northeast. Syria continues to be a weak state. In the absence of effective central government control, the country will remain a plaything for the stronger states in its neighborhood, as it was during the civil war. If Syria’s weakness lures Iran, Israel, Turkey, or the Gulf states back into another round of civil war, the chances for regional stability could vanish.
The prospects for a new Middle East are dim. Iran and Israel—the two countries that have instigated much of the region’s strife in recent decades—are as powerful as ever, and their leaders seem even more set in their beliefs than they were before 2023. Many Arab countries still suffer from the political vacuums that lead to civil war, attract meddlesome outside intervention, and become breeding grounds for armed groups, such as Hamas and Hezbollah, that narrow the already slim prospects for peace.
The Trump administration has made it clear that it is not in the business of building states in the Middle East—a laudable position, given the failures of U.S. efforts to do so in Afghanistan and Iraq. Still, Trump clearly understands that the Middle East will become more stable only if weak Arab states get their acts together. He has lifted sanctions on Syria and embraced its new president. In February 2026, the United States handed over the base it had maintained for years at al-Tanf to the Syrian military, ending a U.S. presence in Syria that dated to 2014. American diplomats worked to de-escalate tensions between Israel and Syria and, before the latest round of fighting, tried to nudge the Lebanese government to take a stiffer stance toward Hezbollah. In June 2026, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a deal, brokered by the United States, that commits Israel to begin handing over control of certain parts of southern Lebanon to the Lebanese armed forces. If the United States tries more forcefully to roll back Israeli interference in Lebanon and Syria, while supporting those governments’ efforts to suppress armed nonstate actors within their borders, the prospects for a more stable region would improve.
How the Trump administration deals with an empowered and ambitious Iranian regime will determine whether the 2026 war is simply another data point in the decades of conflict between the two countries or the beginning of an effort to halt the region’s downward spiral. Any progress toward regional stability will require the United States to keep up its military power in the Gulf. Washington must maintain the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the 5,000 to 10,000 troops deployed in Kuwait, and access to bases in Oman and the United Arab Emirates. Without a U.S. military foothold, Iran can threaten military action against its neighbors at will. The American military presence also reassures the Gulf states of Washington’s commitment to their security after the damage they sustained. That reassurance is necessary to prevent them from simply succumbing out of fear to Iranian pressure on issues such as oil policy and relations with Israel.
