Urban areas are not only the backdrop of crucial political battles. They are also increasingly part of the contestations themselves. Mayors around the globe have found themselves in the cross hairs of illiberal leaders and elected autocrats in their countries. Pushback from local leaders has protected individual rights and the norms and systems of democracy within their jurisdictions and prevented elected authoritarians from fully consolidating their rule. Leaders of American cities should know that they, too, have the power to alter the course of illiberal consolidation.
In fully consolidated autocracies such as China and Russia, cities are assets to national leaders. Led by regime-aligned mayors, they account for a large percentage of economic growth and tax revenue and house the ruling party’s coterie of oligarchs. The elected illiberal autocrats on the rise today, however, cannot count on cities to share their values or priorities. Mayors can present a political threat to those leaders as they attempt to consolidate their rule.
Mayors’ intimate connection with their constituents is one reason why. Surveys consistently find that people around the world trust local leaders more than national ones, regardless of the health of the democracies in which they live. Gallup polls dating back to the 1970s have repeatedly found that nearly 70 percent of Americans trust their local officials, even as trust in the federal government has steadily fallen to a five-decade low, from 70 percent in 1972 to 38 percent today. Data from the research agency Eurofound similarly show that the local governments of EU countries are substantially more popular than the national governments. The dynamic appears to be global: a 2024 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development survey of 30 countries found higher levels of trust in local governments than in national governments.
It is no surprise, then, that mayors often challenge illiberal leaders and candidates in national elections. Ekrem Imamoglu, the mayor of Istanbul popular for his programs that serve low-income women and children, was nominated by the Turkish opposition Republican People’s Party to run against strongman President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in the 2028 elections. In Poland, Warsaw Mayor Rafal Trzaskowski ran for president in 2020 and 2025 against candidates backed by the Law and Justice party, which had been systematically dismantling Poland’s checks and balances, including its independent media and judiciary, since rising to power in 2015.
National governments often mobilize their machinery to thwart these challenges. Days before Imamoglu’s nomination, Istanbul University revoked the mayor’s diploma, making him ineligible by Turkish law to contest the presidency. Then prosecutors charged Imamoglu with 142 offenses, including criminal organization, espionage, and extortion, which carry a total jail term of over 2,000 years. According to reports from Turkish news outlets, Erdogan’s government has detained 20 other mayors on similarly spurious charges. Poland’s state media smeared Trzaskowski during his first presidential run in 2020 as representing a “powerful foreign lobby” linked to George Soros; a Polish media monitoring organization later found that 87 percent of state broadcasts about Trzaskowski were negative, compared with the nearly 100 percent positive broadcasts about Trzaskowski’s opponent, Polish President Andrzej Duda. And in President Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela, Leopoldo López, a mayor from a municipality within Caracas, was barred from running for higher office.
Mayors often draw the ire of elected authoritarian leaders even when they are not vying for national office. During local elections in 2023, Mozambique’s ruling Frelimo party had Manuel de Araujo, the opposition mayor of the port city of Quelimane, arrested and detained on evidence-free charges that he was disturbing the vote-counting process. In Bulgaria, mass demonstrations protesting the arrest of Varna Mayor Blagomir Kotsev in July 2025 did little to dissuade Prime Minister Rosen Zhelyazkov from targeting the country’s cities. The central government continues to punish Vassil Terziev, the popular pro-European mayor of Sofia, by defunding the municipal budget and auditing the city’s finances at an unprecedented rate.
It can be dangerous to be an opposition mayor under an illiberal government. In 2019, amid a media campaign attacking him as “immoral” for his support of gay rights, Pawel Adamowicz, the mayor of Gdansk, Poland (the birthplace of the Solidarity movement), was fatally stabbed at a Christmas celebration by a man analysts suggested was influenced by the Law and Justice government’s hateful rhetoric. During Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte’s six years in power, police officers and masked gunmen killed some 28 mayors. Duterte would know the power of mayors: he served as mayor of Davao City for two decades prior to his entry into national politics.
Trusted, popular mayors enable cities to act as democratic strongholds that can prevent an elected autocrat from fully consolidating power. Cities birthed democracy, and they still protect it. The Athenian statesman Cleisthenes pioneered a democratic system around 500 BC by introducing sweeping reforms to give adult men direct political power. Independent city-states such as Corinth and Sparta adopted the Athenian formula, laying the foundations for popular civic engagement.
Most mayors who operate in elected authoritarian systems, irrespective of their political leanings, protect basic democratic functions as part of their daily work: they issue permits for protests, protect houses of worship, cooperate with civil society, respond to the essential needs of their constituents, and often oversee elections. Some, at great personal risk, create civic spaces that bridge differences and give the public a platform to defy authoritarian tactics of division.
After national legislation outlawed Budapest’s annual Pride parade in 2025, Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s government filed charges against Mayor Gergely Karacsony for organizing the event in defiance of the mandate.In response to the Spanish government’s 2015 Ley Mordaza, which human rights groups dubbed the “Gag Law” for its extensive restrictions on public protest and freedom of speech, Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau turned city-owned buildings into legal sanctuaries for activists protesting the law.
At their best, cities show citizens that government can deliver on making their lives safer and better, in part by creating new ways to involve people in governing. The city government of Gdansk funds high schools to run student contests around future improvements. Bologna, Italy, has established collaboration pacts that allow residents to co-manage public parks and abandoned buildings and created labs where citizens co-design urban projects and directly allocate municipal funds toward the initiatives. And cities across the world have run “participatory budgeting” programs in which residents directly decide how to allocate a portion of the municipal budget.
As Americans and others grow more alienated from increasingly complex and logjammed national bureaucracies, cities allow them to see democracy at work up close. A city government’s progress—or the lack thereof—is often clearly visible. As the public response to messaging-savvy mayors such as New York City’s Zohran Mamdani has demonstrated, even small improvements can be powerful antidotes to the cynicism, apathy, and submission that elected authoritarians seek.
When hostile central governments threaten cities directly, municipal leaders can contest the worst overreaches. Mayors can use municipal resources to restrict or defy the predatory actions of a central government. In 2019, mayors and city councils across the United Kingdom removed central government Home Office immigration officers who had been embedded within their local offices and had used access to municipal databases to build deportation lists. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro attempted to outlaw social-distancing measures, large municipalities such as Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo developed their own guidance instead. Often, mayors work hand in hand with the very civil society groups that illiberal leaders hope to co-opt or destroy. Warsaw and other cities in Poland have created permanent centers for these groups to gather, sometimes alongside city staff.
Cities can also support peaceful protests that spark the mass public support needed to overcome ruling parties’ built-in advantages in free but not fair national elections. Despite Hungary’s national ban, the turnout for the 2025 Budapest Pride Parade was ten times the size it had been typically. Hundreds of thousands took to the streets, accompanied by European mayors and delegations invited by the city in part as a measure to protect protesters against possible violence from regime-aligned law enforcement. Analysts noted that the open defiance helped shatter what the scholar Lorinc Redei has called Orban’s “aura of invincibility” and drive the voter turnout—close to 80 percent, the highest since Hungary’s transition to democracy in 1989—that defeated Orban in 2026.
In Warsaw, Trzaskowski used digital signs at bus stations and walked with marchers in support of a women’s strike protesting the passage of a draconian national abortion law. The largest public protests against the Polish government since the fall of communism in 1989, they played a major role in the Law and Justice government’s loss in the 2023 elections. Protests in Varna against Kotsev’s arrest helped trigger even larger nationwide protests that collapsed Bulgaria’s governing coalition in December 2025.
Even when mayor-led protests do not lead to the ouster of national governments, they can leave a lasting impression on the authoritarians who lead them. Denis Obando, the popular mayor of Nueva Guinea and a member of Nicaragua’s opposition Liberal Party, explicitly organized his municipality against strongman President Daniel Ortega’s electoral machine during local elections in 2012. When Ortega artificially flipped the vote tallies to hand the town to the ruling Sandinista National Liberation Front, Obando and his supporters took to the streets, using physical ballot counts as proof of fraud to challenge the regime’s control.
When López was banned by the Chávez regime from running for public office in 2008, he brought the government to the human rights court of the Organization of American States and called on Venezuelans to protest the election of President Nicolás Maduro, Chávez’s successor. The Maduro regime, which imprisoned López for seven years in solitary confinement for a speech he gave criticizing the Venezuelan strongman, was all too aware of the power of a charismatic local leader: prosecutors accused López of having the ability to send subliminal messages to Venezuelans, impelling them to protest.
In a hyperconnected world, collaboration among cities across borders is now essential for local leaders. Foreign direct investment and trade promotion create jobs, and cities everywhere face similar imperatives to lower energy prices, deliver cleaner air, respond to pandemics, and plan for extreme weather events. This new municipal multilateralism usually involves exchanging best practices for how to address these challenges. With authoritarianism on the rise, cities are now also sharing strategies and participating in collective action against democratic backsliding.
In 2019, the mayors of Bratislava, Budapest, Prague, and Warsaw came together to form the Pact of Free Cities to protect and promote the “common values of freedom, human dignity, democracy, equality, rule of law, social justice, tolerance and cultural diversity.” These Visegrad cities have since expanded the network to include dozens of additional cities, including 11 from the United States.
Pact cities coordinated assistance when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine, sending supplies and welcoming refugees. Warsaw’s mayor recently sent Kyiv electricity generators after continued Russian bombing of the city’s energy grid. When Imamoglu was arrested last year, the pact issued a statement of solidarity signed by 24 prominent mayors, some of whom traveled to Istanbul. The show of municipal solidarity helped pierce the Erdogan government’s narrative that the mayor was a corrupt spy.
U.S. mayors are new to this fight, but they, too, are marshaling their power to push back. Los Angeles and many other cities have channeled funds and resources to groups organizing protection campaigns for residents at risk of deportation. Boston, Chicago, and Philadelphia have taken the Trump administration to court dozens of times, successfully challenging its defunding of local programs, its immigration enforcement tactics, and more. They are finding their voices, as well. Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s testimony before Congress, in March 2025, was one of the earliest examples of official public resistance to the Trump administration’s second-term agenda. The U.S. Conference of Mayors has since issued statements about the administration’s indiscriminate tariff regime and ICE deployments. “As American mayors representing cities large and small—Republican, Democratic and Independent—we state today with a united voice that this turmoil must come to an end,” the organization announced in January, after the deaths of two protesters in Minneapolis. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey has warned his colleagues that if they don’t speak out, their city will be next.
Bass, Wu, Frey, and their peers have had no choice but to learn quickly under fire. But they can take lessons from their international counterparts on what has worked in the past and what federal pressure might yet come. To withstand the next two and a half years, American cities need to band together. Mayors can begin by petitioning a new Congress in January 2027 to restrain ICE enforcement and to restore funding for vital programs. And when Trump eventually leaves office, groups such as the U.S. Conference of Mayors and the National League of Cities should take a page from the Association of Hungarian Local Governments, which was ready to begin conversations with the new government about the restoration of their authority and funding as soon as Orban’s successor, Peter Magyar, declared victory.
Ultimately, the funding cities need for essential services should not be held captive by the federal government. Again taking cues from abroad, U.S. cities should advocate for creative changes to the tax code that allow them to keep more of the money they generate in federal income tax, alongside local levies. Warsaw, for example, keeps near 50 percent, and Brazilian cities are guaranteed 22.5 percent share of federal taxes collected. Insulating municipal budgets, which are often already insufficient, will protect essential services to city residents from the future authoritarians who might target municipalities.
With more and more people coming to live in cities across the world, the urban-national struggle will remain a feature of global politics as long as illiberalism remains on the rise. In the near future, mayors in countries led by illiberal elected autocrats should expect more suppression. But when those autocrats are finally deposed, cities, which have kept the flame of liberty lit, will help rebuild democracy again.
articles.summary: Despots hate cities and the mayors who run them.

articles.title: The Gulf’s China Problem
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
MOHAMMED ALSUDAIRI is Lecturer in the Politics and International Relations of the Arabic Speaking World at the Center for Arab and Islamic Studies at the Australian National University and a Senior Nonresident Fellow at the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies.
ANDREA GHISELLI is Lecturer in International Politics at the University of Exeter and Head of Research at the TOChina Hub’s ChinaMed Project.
AARON GLASSERMAN is a Distinguished Fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University.
The war in Iran has unsettled the Gulf. Arab states are increasingly frustrated with the United States, which, after launching a war that wreaked havoc on global energy markets, failed to keep them safe from Iranian strikes. But the war is also forcing these countries to reassess their relationship with China. Beijing’s wait-and-see approach to the war and unwillingness to use its leverage over Tehran to contain the conflict have disabused Gulf Arab states of any lingering expectation that China could become an important security partner in the foreseeable future.
In the past few years, Gulf Arab states had come to see Beijing as a constructive force in the region. In 2023, about 36 percent of China’s total crude oil imports came from Gulf Cooperation Council countries (Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain); and in 2024, Gulf trade with China reached nearly $300 billion, exceeding trade with the European Union and the United States combined. Many governments in the region anticipated that as Beijing’s economic engagement deepened, it would become more willing to restrain Iranian aggression to protect its local interests and stabilize the region.
Gulf Arab states are now realizing that China is even less likely than before the Iran war to take on responsibility for keeping the Gulf safe. Beijing lacks a vision for what the regional security order should be, and the chaos of the war has reinforced for China that its long-standing strategy of avoiding security commitments or taking sides is the best approach. Although China will continue to build commercial and investment ties in the region, Gulf Arab countries are being forced to accept that Beijing will not counterbalance Washington in ensuring regional security. They must now choose between more fully embracing a volatile United States and searching for new partners to replace what they had hoped China could become.
As China’s presence expanded in the Gulf since the beginning of this decade, expectations were high for what it could do for the region. Although many Gulf Arab states continued to look to Washington as their primary security guarantor, they were optimistic that Beijing was also going to contribute to their protection.
China was becoming increasingly reliant on the Gulf for energy and capital, which Gulf Arab states hoped would make Beijing more invested in safeguarding the region. Prior to the outbreak of the Iran war, in February, Gulf Cooperation Council countries exported nearly four million barrels of crude oil to China each day. Regional sovereign wealth funds were investing heavily in China and opening offices in Beijing, Hong Kong, and Shanghai; and numerous Gulf countries signed cooperation agreements with China in sectors including renewable energy and space technology. The Chinese diaspora in the Arabian Peninsula was also growing, reaching more than half a million.
Beijing’s influence in Tehran provided hope that China could temper Iran’s belligerence toward its neighbors. Iran is heavily reliant on China for economic and diplomatic support because of Washington’s long-standing sanctions. In 2021, the two countries signed a 25-year comprehensive cooperation agreement, which signaled China’s willingness to expand its investments in Iran. China’s leverage over Iran was a factor in Saudi Arabia’s willingness to have Beijing act as guarantor of the agreement that Riyadh signed with Tehran, in 2023, which reestablished diplomatic ties between the two Gulf powers. China, Iran, and Saudi Arabia held three subsequent trilateral meetings, most recently in Tehran in December 2025, which were rare moments of diplomatic optimism in the region.
China’s words and deeds further contributed to Gulf expectations that China would become a regional security stakeholder. After a decade of pessimism following the Arab Spring, which saw the Middle East mired in intense fighting and proxy wars, China saw promise in a new generation of policymakers and reformers. Many Gulf leaders seemed determined to diversify their sources of growth, wean their economies off oil, and enhance their connections with their neighbors—goals that fit Beijing’s strengths and to which China was willing to lend support. Chinese state media published glowing profiles of rulers in the region, including Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom they described as pursuing “Chinese-style modernization.”
Meanwhile, China accelerated its diplomatic engagement with the Gulf. In 2022, Chinese leader Xi Jinping attended the first China–Arab States Summit and a China–Gulf Cooperation Council Summit held in Riyadh, where he signed a joint statement acknowledging the UAE’s territorial claims to three disputed islands controlled by Iran. In March 2023, Chinese analysts and officials heralded the détente between Saudi Arabia and Iran as the beginning of a “tide of reconciliation” that would overcome years of conflict, stagnation, and unrest.
Gulf Arab states also assumed that growing Chinese interests in the region would increase pressure on the United States to maintain its primacy and make it easier for them to gain economic and security concessions from Washington. The Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei, for instance, maintains major operational hubs in Dubai and Riyadh, and U.S. efforts to force Gulf Arab states to divest from it failed because of a lack of viable alternatives. Growing U.S.-Chinese technology competition provided Washington with an additional reason to support the region. In May 2025, after U.S. President Donald Trump toured the Gulf, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia signed ambitious deals to procure chips from the U.S. technology company Nvidia, a necessary step toward achieving their goal of becoming artificial intelligence powerhouses. Gulf Arab states were optimistic that having two external powers interested in the region would offer them more options and enhance their overall security.
But the violence of the past three years has dashed Gulf Arab states’ hopes about China, an assessment that officials and analysts in the region have frequently shared in conversations. Since the Hamas attack on Israel, in October 2023, China has shown no intention of shouldering a meaningful regional security burden. Although Beijing postured as a peacemaker and mediated talks between warring parties—in July 2024, for instance, it organized a meeting of various Palestinian political factions—the attempts remained superficial and did nothing to change the status quo. In late 2023, when the Houthis began striking commercial and military vessels in the Red Sea, China did not pressure Iran to rein in its proxy’s attacks on global shipping; instead, it negotiated a private agreement with the Houthis to secure the safety of Chinese-flagged ships.
During this year’s Iran war, China again declined to use its considerable leverage over Iran to keep the Iranians from attacking China’s Gulf partners—a move that especially concerned Saudi Arabia, which felt that Beijing should come to its defense because China was the guarantor of its reconciliation with Tehran. Although China mostly refrained from supporting Iran against U.S. and Israeli attacks, some Gulf states viewed China as complicit in Iran’s attacks on the Gulf because it vetoed a UN Security Council resolution calling for an international force to protect shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and because of reports that Chinese companies may have provided geospatial intelligence to help Tehran hit regional targets more accurately.
Beijing’s restraint was driven by both pragmatism and paralysis. Since the Arab Spring in 2010–11 and the expansion of the Islamic State (also known as ISIS) in the years that followed, Chinese policymakers and scholars have debated whether and how Beijing should change its behavior in the Middle East. Critics of the government’s policy argued that as a great power, China needed to do more to protect its interests and ensure regional stability. But they failed to elaborate what a different strategy would look like on the ground, when to potentially involve China’s military, and how to handle the costs of forging a deeper partnership with a regional power such as Saudi Arabia. For a turbulent region—and one with a long history of costly foreign interventions—leaders in Beijing seemingly decided that doing nothing remained the best option.
Chinese policymakers were also cautious because they were unsure where the region was headed. Beijing felt that the restoration of Iranian-Saudi diplomatic relations, for instance, burnished its image as a responsible power at very little cost. But the fall of Bashar al-Assad in Syria, in 2024, and the 12-day war, in 2025, raised concern that the region would descend into chaos. As a result, when the United States and Israel started bombing Iran in February, Beijing did not have a clearly articulated alternative plan to protect its economic assets and minimize the chances of being dragged into protracted conflict. The resulting hesitancy to act meant sidelining Gulf concerns and leaving them vulnerable to Iranian attacks.
The Gulf is not going to give up on China completely. Gulf-Chinese relations will continue to expand in areas in which both sides have clear expectations, concrete interests, and limited political risks. Energy will be at the heart of ongoing ties. In the short term, Gulf countries will continue to export large amounts of oil to China. In the long term, as more of the world decarbonizes its energy supply and pursues electrification, China’s leadership in green technology will make it a key partner for Gulf Arab countries that want to undertake their own transition to renewable energy—a process that is already underway. Gulf states’ sovereign wealth funds are also likely to increase their portfolios in China, which wants more capital investment in its markets; at the same time, Chinese companies are funding mining and construction projects in the Gulf. China offers money, technological know-how, and industrial logistics capabilities that Gulf governments want and need to pursue their ambitions, especially in areas including drones, hydroponic agriculture, and robotics.
But the war has shown that China’s ongoing economic interests do not translate into help securing the region. This means that for Gulf Arab states, the United States is the only power capable of maintaining regional security—but is also the one most likely to destabilize it. Beijing’s unwillingness to play a larger role is forcing Gulf Arab states to make hard choices on how to protect themselves.
They are divided on the best way forward. Countries including Oman and Saudi Arabia, uneasy about overreliance on Washington, are pursuing new hedging strategies. Oman—which, in June, Trump threatened to bomb—has most forcefully called for balancing support from Washington by increasing regional security cooperation: in an article published in the French newspaper Le Monde on July 13, Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi called for the creation of a post-American security order that would include the Gulf monarchies, Iran, and Iraq. Countries such as Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, however, are drawing closer to the United States. Without other viable patrons to protect them, and facing intense Iranian assaults, these states see moving deeper into Washington’s orbit as the safest option. But even the countries that want to take cover under the U.S. security umbrella are also investing in their own defenses, opening dialogues with Iran to reduce tensions, and reaching out to countries such as Turkey and Pakistan to establish additional security partnerships. Without being able to turn to China, they are pursuing whatever options are available in case the bet on Washington fails completely.
As Gulf Arab states search for other ways to protect themselves, China’s interest in getting more actively involved in securing the region is further decreasing. Beijing can maintain valuable economic ties with even fewer risks of security entanglements. The Gulf-Chinese relationship is increasingly resembling the Iranian-Chinese relationship: it is becoming a partnership sustained by necessity rather than by rising expectations. The only upshot for Gulf Arab countries is that because they have more to offer China economically than Iran does, when the war ends they will still find themselves in a far more favorable dynamic with Beijing.
articles.summary: Beijing wants trade but not responsibility.
